learningObjectives: Identify the key components of Pega application security including the AIC Triad, Security Checklist, and guardrail compliance.
Describe authentication vs. authorization and the three authorization models: RBAC, ABAC, and CBAC.

elements.text: Think of Pega app security like an airport: Authentication is the passport check at the border (WHO are you?). Authorization is the boarding pass (WHAT zones can you enter?). The Security Checklist is the pre-flight safety checklist — the plane (app) cannot take off (deploy to production) until every box is checked.

elements.description: Availability, Integrity, Confidentiality — Pega's shared security goal. Unauthorized individuals cannot access or modify the application or its data. Authorized individuals only access what they need to perform their jobs.

A guideline Rule instance automatically installed per app version to harden Pega applications. Tasks are organized by timing and key area: monitoring, authentication, authorization, auditing, production testing. Not all tasks are required for every app.

Deployment Manager BLOCKS production deployment if the Security Checklist is not completed. This is a hard block — not a soft warning. On Pega Cloud, some environment setup steps are done automatically under the Service Agreement.

The MOST IMPORTANT security requirement for any Pega application. Pega Platform's built-in security features may NOT be successfully enforced when custom code is used. Always use Pega's built-in security configuration — never rely on custom code for security enforcement.

elements.description: Application-level security: protects from outsiders and unauthorized users (passwords, auth policies, MFA, third-party tools). Feature security: controls what authorized users can and cannot access within the app (RBAC, ABAC, CBAC).

App Studio: Authentication landing page → Security Policies tab. Dev Studio: Configure → Org & Security → Authentication → Security Policies (applies to the entire Pega Platform server). CAUTION: authentication service settings may OVERRIDE these page settings.
Sets rules for password strength: minimum length, required character types (uppercase, digits, symbols), and restrictions on predictable or reused passwords.
Presents a challenge on initial login or after failed login attempts. Can use a custom or default CAPTCHA.

studyGuide.sectionTitle: Security Policies — Access Control and Monitoring

elements.description: ENABLED: penalty period in seconds that increases automatically with each repeated failure. DISABLED: account locks after N failed attempts for N minutes.
Controls the level of detail recorded in the system log for security-related events.

Requires a time-limited one-time password (OTP) delivered via email or SMS after initial credential entry. Two-factor authentication (2FA) is a SUBSET of MFA — MFA is the broader category requiring two or more evidence factors.
Automatically disables access for users who have been inactive for a specified number of days. An exclusion list can protect users who still require access despite inactivity.

elements.description: Pega's first line of defense. Credentials: Operator ID (email) + password. Advanced options: SAML 2.0, OpenID Connect, token credentials → enable Single Sign-On (SSO). Auth service Rule configures MFA and SSO policies.
Controls what authenticated users can access and perform within the application. Three models: RBAC, ABAC, and CBAC.
Role-Based Access Control. Users are grouped into Roles; permissions are assigned per Role. Simplest model — access is determined by job role.

Attribute-Based Access Control. Access is determined by comparing object characteristics (Case, field, document) to user attributes. More granular than RBAC — the same role can have different access depending on contextual attributes.
Client-Based Access Control. Tracks and processes requests to view, update, or remove personal customer data. Designed to address GDPR and similar data privacy regulations.

examPitfalls.title: AIC — correct order and acronym
examPitfalls.trapDescription: An exam question asks candidates to select the correct Pega security triad from a list containing CIA, AIC, and CAI. Candidates default to the industry-standard CIA — Pega uses its own AIC ordering.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Memorize: AIC = Availability, Integrity, Confidentiality. Pega uses this specific acronym and order.

examPitfalls.title: Security Checklist failure BLOCKS deployment — not just a warning
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A scenario asks what happens when Deployment Manager detects an incomplete Security Checklist. Candidates select 'generates a warning but deployment continues' — not knowing deployment is hard-blocked.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Deployment Manager BLOCKS production deployment if the Security Checklist is not completed. This is a hard enforcement — the app cannot go live.

examPitfalls.title: Guardrail compliance is the #1 security requirement
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Questions ask which single security requirement is most important. Candidates pick MFA or the Security Checklist. Guardrail compliance ranks highest because custom code can break Pega's built-in security mechanisms.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Guardrail compliance is the most important requirement. Pega's security features may not work correctly when custom code is used — always use built-in Pega security.

examPitfalls.title: Auth service settings can OVERRIDE Security Policies page settings
examPitfalls.trapDescription: A question describes conflicting values between Auth service and the Security Policies page, asking which wins. Candidates assume Security Policies page always takes precedence — Auth service settings can override it.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Settings configured for a specific authentication service may OVERRIDE the Security Policies page settings — always check auth service configuration.

examPitfalls.title: 2FA is a SUBSET of MFA — not the same thing
examPitfalls.trapDescription: An exam question asks whether 2FA and MFA are equivalent. Candidates select 'Yes — they require the same number of factors.' MFA is the broader category (two OR more); 2FA is a specific subset requiring exactly two.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: Two-factor authentication (2FA) requires exactly two evidence factors — it is a subset of MFA. MFA is the broader category requiring two or more factors.

examPitfalls.title: ABAC vs. CBAC — different purposes
examPitfalls.trapDescription: Questions ask when to use Attribute-Based Access Control vs. Class-Based Access Control. Candidates say they are interchangeable. CBAC controls access to entire rule classes (who can see what type of record); ABAC adds field-level conditions based on data attributes — they operate at different granularities.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: ABAC: access determined by comparing object characteristics (Case, field, document) to user attributes. CBAC: designed specifically for GDPR — handles requests to view, update, or remove personal customer data.

examPitfalls.title: Security Policies navigation: App Studio ≠ Dev Studio path
examPitfalls.trapDescription: An exam question asks for the Dev Studio navigation path to Security Policies. Candidates describe the App Studio path (Authentication landing page → Security Policies tab) and lose marks for swapping the two paths.
examPitfalls.bestPractice: App Studio: Authentication landing page → Security Policies tab. Dev Studio: Configure → Org & Security → Authentication → Security Policies (applies to the entire Pega Platform server).

practiceQuiz.scenario: An SA is reviewing security fundamentals for a new Pega application with a team and introduces the AIC triad as the framework for evaluating the application's security posture. In Pega security terminology, what does AIC stand for?
practiceQuiz.hint: Pega's shared security goal with clients — not CIA.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Pega's security model is built around the AIC triad: Availability (the system is accessible when needed), Integrity (data is accurate and not tampered with), and Confidentiality (sensitive data is protected from unauthorized access). Pega deliberately uses the order AIC rather than the more common CIA acronym used in general cybersecurity frameworks — a distinction frequently tested on the exam.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A project team finishes developing a Pega application but has not completed the Security Checklist. What happens when they try to deploy to production?

options.text: A warning is displayed but deployment proceeds
The application deploys with limited functionality
An email notification is sent to the security team

practiceQuiz.hint: The Security Checklist has a hard enforcement mechanism.
practiceQuiz.rationale: In Pega, an incomplete Security Checklist is a hard blocker — the Deployment Manager will not allow the pipeline to promote the application to production until every item on the checklist is addressed. This is not a soft warning that can be overridden. Teams must resolve all flagged items before any production deployment can proceed.

practiceQuiz.scenario: What is the MOST IMPORTANT security requirement for any Pega Platform application?
practiceQuiz.hint: Pega security features may not work when custom code is used.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Guardrail compliance is the most important security requirement. Pega's built-in security features may not be enforced when custom code overrides them — developers must always use built-in Pega security configuration.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An SA wants to configure Security Policies for the entire Pega Platform server using Dev Studio. What is the correct navigation path?

options.text: Configure → Org & Security → Authentication → Security Policies
App Studio → Authentication landing page → Security Policies tab
Dev Studio → Records → Security → Policy Manager

practiceQuiz.hint: Dev Studio path applies settings to the entire Pega Platform server.
practiceQuiz.rationale: In Dev Studio: Configure → Org & Security → Authentication → Security Policies. App Studio uses the Authentication landing page → Security Policies tab. Both lead to security policy configuration but via different paths.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which security policy automatically disables access for users who have been inactive for a specified number of days?
practiceQuiz.hint: This security policy targets operators who have been inactive for a specified number of days.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Operator disablement auto-disables users inactive for N days. An exclusion list can protect users who still need access. Lockout is for failed login attempts. Audit controls log detail. CAPTCHA is a login challenge.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A client wants users to receive a time-limited one-time password via email after entering their credentials. Which security policy configures this?
practiceQuiz.hint: A second piece of evidence delivered by email or SMS.
practiceQuiz.rationale: MFA uses a time-limited OTP via email or SMS. 2FA is a subset of MFA. Password policy controls complexity. CAPTCHA is a bot detection challenge. Lockout prevents brute force by adding penalty time.

practiceQuiz.scenario: The lockout policy is ENABLED with an initial penalty period of 30 seconds. After the second failed login attempt, what happens to the penalty period?

options.text: The penalty period increases automatically with each repeated failure
The penalty stays fixed at 30 seconds for all failures
The account is permanently locked after the second failure
The penalty resets to zero after each failed attempt

practiceQuiz.hint: Enabled lockout escalates the penalty on repeat failures.
practiceQuiz.rationale: When lockout is ENABLED, the penalty period in seconds increases automatically with each repeated login failure. DISABLED mode locks the account for N minutes after N failed attempts.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A BA is explaining authentication methods to a security-conscious client stakeholder. How does two-factor authentication (2FA) relate to multi-factor authentication (MFA) in Pega's security model?

options.text: 2FA is a subset of MFA — exactly two evidence factors
MFA is a subset of 2FA — MFA extends 2FA
They are the same concept with different names
2FA applies only to external users; MFA applies to all operators

practiceQuiz.hint: Recall how two-factor authentication relates to the broader multi-factor authentication category.
practiceQuiz.rationale: 2FA is a SUBSET of MFA where users provide exactly two pieces of evidence. MFA is the broader category requiring two or more factors. They are not the same.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which THREE authentication protocols can be used to enable Single Sign-On (SSO) in Pega Platform?
practiceQuiz.hint: CAPTCHA is a login challenge — not an SSO protocol.
practiceQuiz.rationale: SAML 2.0, OpenID Connect, and token credentials all enable SSO in Pega. CAPTCHA challenges whether the login attempt is human — it is not an authentication protocol for SSO.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A security review team is asking a Pega SA to clearly distinguish between authentication and authorization during an access control design review. Which aspect of application access does authentication specifically address?

options.text: WHO can access the application — Pega's first line of defense
WHAT users can do after they gain access
Which Case Types users can create
Which data fields users can view or edit

practiceQuiz.hint: Authentication answers WHO you are; Authorization answers WHAT you are allowed to do.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Authentication answers WHO can access the application and is Pega's first line of defense. B, C, and D are all aspects of authorization (WHAT users can do after gaining access).

practiceQuiz.scenario: Which authorization model determines access by comparing characteristics of an object (such as a Case or field) to attributes of the requesting user?
practiceQuiz.hint: Attribute-based access considers object characteristics vs user attributes — that is ABAC.
practiceQuiz.rationale: ABAC compares object characteristics (Case, field, document) to user attributes to determine access. RBAC is role-based. CBAC handles personal data / GDPR compliance. FBAC is not a valid Pega authorization model.

practiceQuiz.scenario: Your organization must comply with EU GDPR and needs to handle requests to view, update, or remove personal customer data held in Pega. Which authorization model addresses this?
practiceQuiz.hint: Personal data requests / GDPR compliance = CBAC.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Authentication verifies identity (WHO you are). Authorization controls permissions (WHAT you can access). Security Policies in Pega configure both — but they are distinct layers of the security model.

practiceQuiz.scenario: A business stakeholder asks an SA to explain the difference between authentication and authorization in Pega. Which TWO statements are correct?

options.text: Authentication verifies who the user is — confirming their identity before granting access to the system
Authorization determines what an authenticated user is permitted to do within the application
Authentication and authorization are both managed exclusively through the Pega Security Checklist tool
Authorization occurs before authentication — Pega evaluates permissions before confirming a user's identity

practiceQuiz.hint: Authentication = who you are; Authorization = what you can do. Authentication always comes first.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Authentication is the process of verifying a user's identity (e.g., username/password, SSO, MFA). Authorization happens after successful authentication and determines what resources and actions the user can access. Authentication always precedes authorization, and both are managed through multiple Pega mechanisms, not solely through the Security Checklist.

practiceQuiz.scenario: An SA is reviewing the authorization models supported by Pega Platform. Which TWO authorization model types are valid in Pega?

options.text: Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) — permissions are granted based on the user's assigned Access Role
Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) — permissions are evaluated based on attributes of the user, resource, or environment
Biometric-Based Access Control (BBAC) — permissions are granted based on fingerprint or facial recognition scan results
Temporal-Based Access Control (TBAC) — permissions are exclusively determined by a fixed schedule with no role evaluation

practiceQuiz.hint: Pega supports three authorization models: RBAC, ABAC, and CBAC. Biometric and temporal-only are not Pega models.
practiceQuiz.rationale: Pega Platform supports three authorization models: RBAC (permissions via Access Roles), ABAC (permissions based on evaluated attributes of user, resource, or environment), and CBAC (Claim-Based Access Control). Biometric-Based and Temporal-Based Access Control are not Pega authorization model categories.

quickRecap.value: Availability, Integrity, Confidentiality — Pega's shared security goal (not CIA).
Deployment Manager BLOCKS production if not completed. Tasks: monitoring, authentication, authorization, auditing, production testing.
MOST IMPORTANT security requirement — use built-in Pega security, never custom code.
Password, CAPTCHA, Lockout (penalty grows), Audit (log detail), MFA (OTP email/SMS), Operator disablement (inactive users).
App Studio: Authentication landing page → Security Policies tab. Dev Studio: Configure → Org & Security → Authentication → Security Policies.
Specific auth service settings may OVERRIDE Security Policies page settings.
2FA is a SUBSET of MFA. MFA = two or more factors. 2FA = exactly two.
Authentication = WHO can access (Operator ID + password; SSO: SAML 2.0/OpenID Connect/tokens). Authorization = WHAT they can do.
RBAC (job roles), ABAC (object attributes vs user attributes), CBAC (personal data / GDPR compliance).
